title: Structural typing, assignability and variance
summary: Why TypeScript accepts some assignments and rejects others: structural compatibility, excess property checks on fresh object literals, covariant arrays, contravariant function parameters under strictFunctionTypes, method bivariance and the in/out variance annotations.
prerequisiteNotes: ts-generics: type parameters and constraints, which variance talks about. ts-narrowing-unions: union types and the idea of one type being narrower than another.
objectives: Explain structural typing and predict whether one object type is assignable to another.
Say when excess property checks fire and why they disappear once a literal is stored in a variable.
Describe covariance and contravariance with arrays and function parameters, including the hole that mutable arrays leave open.
Explain why method shorthand parameters stay bivariant under strictFunctionTypes and when to prefer function properties.
Read and write the in and out variance annotations on generic type parameters.

concepts.title: Structural typing and excess property checks
concepts.body: TypeScript compares types by their **shape**, not their name. A value is assignable to `Point` when it has at least the members `Point` needs with compatible types; extra members are fine, so a `{ x, y, z }` object can be passed where `{ x, y }` is expected. The one exception is a **fresh object literal** written straight into a typed position: there, an unknown key is almost always a typo, so the compiler reports an excess property error. Store the literal in a variable first and the freshness is gone, the extra key is accepted and it still exists at runtime, which matters if you serialize the value.

concepts.title: Covariance: arrays and return types
concepts.body: A type constructor is **covariant** when it keeps the direction of subtyping: if `Dog` is assignable to `Animal`, then `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]` and `() => Dog` to `() => Animal`. That is sound for things you only read. Mutable arrays are both read and written, so covariance is a known hole: after `const animals: Animal[] = dogs`, `animals.push(cat)` compiles and puts a cat in the dog array. Prefer `readonly Dog[]` (or `ReadonlyArray<Dog>`) for inputs you do not mutate; a readonly array has no `push`, so the hole cannot be used.

concepts.title: Contravariance: function parameters and strictFunctionTypes
concepts.body: Parameters flip the direction. A handler that accepts any `Animal` can safely stand in for one that will only ever be called with a `Dog`, but not the other way round: a `Dog` handler might call `bark()` on a cat. With `strictFunctionTypes` (part of `strict`), parameters of **function types** are checked **contravariantly**. Parameters of **method shorthand** (`accept(value: T): void` inside an interface or class) are still checked **bivariantly**, either direction is accepted, because many built-in types such as `Array` rely on it. Declare callbacks as properties (`accept: (value: T) => void`) when you want the strict check.

concepts.title: Variance annotations: in, out and invariance
concepts.body: TypeScript works out the variance of each type parameter by measuring how it is used. Since TypeScript 4.7 you can state it with `out T` (covariant: T only appears in output positions), `in T` (contravariant: T only appears in inputs) or `in out T` (invariant: both). The compiler checks the annotation against the structure, so it documents intent, catches accidental changes and can speed up checking of large recursive types. A type that both reads and writes T, like a mutable box with `get` and `set` function properties, is invariant: neither `Box<Dog>` nor `Box<Animal>` is assignable to the other.

walkthrough.title: Reading an assignability error from the top
walkthrough.body: When an assignment fails, the message nests from the outer type down to the first member that does not fit, for example "Type `Handler<Dog>` is not assignable to `Handler<Animal>`… Types of parameters `value` and `value` are incompatible". Read the last line first: it names the exact position. If it mentions parameters, ask which way data flows. If it mentions a property you never wrote, check whether it came from a fresh literal (an excess property) or an intersection.

walkthrough.title: Fixing the hole without casts
walkthrough.body: Each unsound pattern has a type-level fix that avoids `as`. Accept `readonly T[]` when a function only reads a list. Write callbacks as function properties so `strictFunctionTypes` applies. When you must store an object that may carry extra keys, copy only the known keys before sending it anywhere that cares, which is what the warm-up exercise does. Reach for an explicit variance annotation on public generic types, so a later edit that changes variance fails at the declaration and not in some caller.

task: Write `matchesShape(shape, value, exact)`. `shape` maps keys to the `typeof` result each must have, such as `{ id: 'number', name: 'string' }`. Return true when `value` is a non-null, non-array object that has every key with the right `typeof`. Extra keys are allowed (structural typing) unless `exact` is true, in which case any key the shape does not list makes it fail, like an excess property check.
hints: Reject `null`, arrays and primitives first (`typeof null` is `'object'`), then use an own-property check so a key like `toString` is not found on the prototype.
Only do the extra-keys pass when `exact` is true.
checklist: Null, arrays and primitives return false.
A missing key or a wrong typeof returns false.
Extra keys pass when exact is false and fail when it is true.
pitfalls: Assuming an extra key disappears because the type does not mention it; it stays on the object at runtime.
Passing a mutable `Dog[]` into code typed `Animal[]` that pushes into it.
Declaring callbacks with method shorthand and expecting `strictFunctionTypes` to check them.
Using `as` to silence a variance error instead of fixing the direction of the type.

extraPractice.title: Strip the extra keys
extraPractice.prompt: Write `pickKnown(obj, keys)` that returns a new object with only the listed keys that `obj` actually owns. Keys that are missing from `obj` are left out, not set to undefined.
hints: Start from an empty object and copy key by key.
Use an own-property check, not `in`, so prototype keys are ignored.
checklist: Prototype keys such as toString are ignored.

extraPractice.title: Model function assignability
extraPractice.prompt: Types form a small hierarchy: `never` is below everything, `Dog` and `Cat` are below `Animal`, and `Animal` is below `unknown`. A function type is `{ param, ret }`. Write `canAssign(target, source, method)` that says whether `source` can be assigned to `target`: returns are covariant, parameters are contravariant, and when `method` is true parameters are bivariant (either direction is enough).
hints: The helper `isSub(a, b)` already walks the hierarchy; for parameters, ask whether the target's parameter fits into the source's.
Bivariance means `isSub` in either direction, which still rejects unrelated siblings such as Dog and Cat.
checklist: Parameters are contravariant unless method is true.
Unrelated parameter types fail even when bivariant.

followUps.question: Why does TypeScript keep method parameters bivariant even in strict mode?
followUps.answer: Because many widely used types, including `Array<T>`, declare methods whose parameters mention T. Checking them contravariantly would make `Dog[]` not assignable to `Animal[]`, breaking a huge amount of reasonable code. Bivariant methods keep that working; function-typed properties get the strict check.

followUps.question: Why does an excess property error vanish when you assign through a variable?
followUps.answer: Excess property checks only apply to fresh object literals, where an unknown key is almost certainly a typo. Once the literal is in a variable it may legitimately be used elsewhere with all its keys, so ordinary structural assignability applies and extra keys are allowed.

followUps.question: What makes a generic type invariant, and how would you show it?
followUps.answer: T is used in both input and output positions, for example a box with a `get: () => T` and a `set: (value: T) => void`. Neither `Box<Dog>` nor `Box<Animal>` can replace the other safely. You can declare it with `in out T`, and the compiler will reject an assignment in either direction.

takeaways: Compatibility is structural: extra members are fine except on fresh object literals.
Read-only positions are covariant, write-only positions are contravariant, and read-write positions are invariant.
Mutable arrays are covariant for convenience, which is unsound; use readonly arrays for inputs.
strictFunctionTypes checks function-type parameters contravariantly but leaves method shorthand bivariant.
The in and out annotations state variance and are checked against the type's structure.

diagrams.title: Fresh literal versus stored object
diagrams.alt: Two panels. A fresh object literal with an extra key is rejected by the excess property check; the same object stored in a variable first is accepted and keeps the extra key at runtime.
diagrams.caption: Freshness, not the type, decides whether extra keys are reported.

diagrams.title: How a covariant array lets a cat in
diagrams.alt: A flow from a Dog array aliased as an Animal array, through a push of a cat-like animal, to a runtime TypeError when the original Dog array calls bark on it.
diagrams.caption: Both names point at one array; only the type of the alias changed.

diagrams.title: Function property versus method shorthand
diagrams.alt: Two panels. A string-only handler assigned to a function property that accepts string or number is rejected under strictFunctionTypes; the same handler assigned to a method shorthand is accepted because method parameters stay bivariant.
diagrams.caption: Write callbacks as properties to get the contravariant check.

exercises.typeChecks:
type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false
type Expect<T extends true> = T
type _fn = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof canAssign>, [target: Fn, source: Fn, method: boolean]>>
// @ts-expect-error Fish is not a Name
canAssign({ param: 'Fish', ret: 'Dog' }, { param: 'Dog', ret: 'Dog' }, false)

predict.explain: `animals` and `dogs` are the same array. Covariant arrays let the push compile, so `dogs` now holds an object without `bark`.
Assigning through a variable skips the excess property check, and types never remove keys at runtime, so `z` is serialized too.
Method shorthand parameters are bivariant, so the assignment compiles. At runtime `(42).toUpperCase` is undefined and calling it throws a TypeError.

lab.tip: When a variance error confuses you, ask which way the data flows through the type parameter: out of the value (covariant), into it (contravariant) or both (invariant).
